headline: A book excerpt in WIRED says Wikipedia, which has banned AI-written articles, is struggling to keep readers and volunteer editors as AI answers spread.
score_reason: Pool score 5 lowered to 4: an essay-style book excerpt that retells developments from 2024 to March 2026 and reports no new event on 13 Oct.
importance_line: Wikipedia's volunteer editors and the many people who rely on it for checked facts are affected first, then AI companies that draw on it, but the ban's scope and the readership figures are the author's account of earlier sources, and Henner himself doubts AI is the main cause.
summary: WIRED publishes an excerpt from Richard Cooke's book The Last Best Place on the Internet: A Human History of Wikipedia, in which he recounts that Wikipedia's editors banned writing with large language models in March 2026, allowing them only for translation and minor proofreading, and notes that a Princeton University study had found substantial AI-generated content in about 5% of nearly 3,000 new English articles from August 2024. Cooke also cites long-time Wikipedian Christophe Henner's January warning that the encyclopedia has lost almost a quarter of its readership since 2022, although Henner calls AI "an accelerant, not the fire" and points to a wider generational shift away from reading articles.
notes: Full excerpt read. It is a new publication (13 Oct 2026) but retells events from Aug 2024 to Mar 2026, so it is not a fresh news event; the score is lowered by 1. The March 2026 ban and the readership figures are Cooke's account of earlier sources (Henner's January post, Pew, a Princeton study); no primary source was opened.
